blog.title: How Much Does a Small Business Website Cost? Honest Ranges
blog.title_tag: How Much Does a Small Business Website Cost? | ART3RY
blog.meta_description: How much a small business website costs in 2026: honest ranges for DIY, freelancer and agency builds, what drives the price, and what is worth paying for.
blog.dek: Real bands for every route, the running costs nobody mentions until month two, and a checklist you can hold a quote against. No sales gloss, no fake price list.

sections.h2: The short answer
paragraphs: A small business website costs roughly $200 to $500 a year if you build it yourself on a platform like Squarespace or Wix, $1,000 to $5,000 if you hire a freelancer, $2,500 to $10,000 for a done-for-you build from an independent specialist, and $5,000 to $30,000 or more through an agency. Running costs after launch land around $200 to $1,500 a year.

Those are the bands the quotes actually fall into. Inside each one the spread is wide, and the spread is not random. It comes down to who writes the words, whether the design is custom or a good template wearing your brand, what the site has to do besides sit there, and what happens to it after launch.

A five-page site for a business with photos, reviews, and a clear offer already in hand is a genuinely different job from a five-page site for a business that has none of that. Same page count, very different price, and any quote that ignores the difference is guessing.

The rest of this page is the detail: what each route really costs, what you pay every year no matter who builds it, what moves the number up or down, and how to look at a quote you have been given and tell whether it is fair.

sections.h2: The four ways to get a website, and what each really costs
paragraphs: Build it yourself on a website builder. Squarespace, Wix, GoDaddy, Framer, and Shopify all sell a subscription that includes hosting, security certificates, and an editor. Business tiers usually sit somewhere between $16 and $45 a month when you pay annually, and a .com domain adds $10 to $20 a year. Call it $200 to $500 a year in cash. The real cost is your time, and it is the cost everyone leaves out.

Hire a freelancer. For a straightforward small business site this usually runs $1,000 to $5,000 as a one-time build. Under $1,000 you are almost always getting a template filled in with whatever you send over. Above $5,000 you should be getting strategy, copywriting, and someone who asks about your customers before they open a design tool. Experienced freelancers in the United States commonly bill $75 to $150 an hour, and a small site is usually a 20 to 60 hour job.

Done-for-you from an independent specialist. Typically $2,500 to $10,000 for the build, often with a monthly for hosting, updates, and changes. This is the middle route: one accountable person, agency-level output, no account manager between you and the work. It is what I do, and I will come back to the pricing honestly at the end of this page.

Hire an agency. $5,000 to $30,000 and upward for a small business site, with mid-market agencies commonly landing in the $8,000 to $25,000 band. You are paying for a team, a process, and overhead. Sometimes that buys real depth. Sometimes it buys a project manager, a discovery deck, and the same template a freelancer would have used. I wrote about how to tell those apart in [when to fire your marketing agency without losing leads](/blog/marketing-agency-alternative-fire-without-losing-leads/).

sections.h2: What you pay every year, no matter who builds it
paragraphs: The domain. A .com is usually $10 to $20 a year. Watch the renewal price rather than the first-year price, because cheap first years are standard and the renewal is often two or three times higher. Add privacy protection if it is not free. One rule matters more than the price: the domain must be registered in your name, in an account you can log into. Not your builder's account, not your nephew's.

Hosting. Shared hosting is $3 to $15 a month. Managed WordPress hosting is $20 to $50. Static hosting on the modern platforms can genuinely be free for a small business site. If you are on a builder like Squarespace or Wix, hosting is already inside the subscription and there is no separate bill. Security certificates should cost you nothing at this point, and anyone charging you for basic SSL is charging you for something the whole internet gives away.

Business email on your own domain. Roughly $6 to $9 per user per month for the entry business plans from the major providers. This is the cheapest credibility you will ever buy. A quote sent from a free webmail address reads as a side gig, and a quote sent from your own domain reads as a company, and the difference costs you less than a tank of gas per year.

Maintenance. On a builder, near zero. On WordPress, either your own time every month or $50 to $200 a month to someone who keeps plugins current and backups running. On a custom build, whatever your maintenance agreement says. Add whatever changes cost, and get that number in writing before you sign, because ongoing change requests are where a cheap build turns expensive.

sections.h2: What actually moves the price
paragraphs: Who writes the words. This is the single biggest swing and it is almost never discussed at quoting time. If the quote assumes you supply the copy, you are the bottleneck, the project stalls for six weeks, and you end up writing it at midnight anyway. If it includes real copywriting, expect $500 to $3,000 of the total to be that, and expect it to be worth it, because the words are what convert, not the layout.

Custom design versus a customized template. A genuinely custom design costs thousands more and is worth it for a small number of businesses. For most local service businesses a strong template with your real photos, your real reviews, and your real offer will outperform a custom design built on thin content. Pay for content before you pay for uniqueness.

What the site has to do. A brochure site is one price. Add online booking, payments, a client portal, a quote calculator, a members area, or a multi-step intake form, and each one is a system with its own edge cases, its own failure modes, and its own testing. Every feature that touches money or the calendar roughly doubles the care required.

Integrations and photography. Wiring forms into your follow-up, your calendar, and your invoicing is where a website stops being a brochure, and it takes real work. Photography is the other underrated line: a half day with a photographer costs a few hundred dollars and does more for conversion than another round of design revisions. Stock photos are free and every visitor knows exactly what they are looking at.

Page count matters less than people think. A twelve-page site is not three times the work of a four-page site, because the hard part is the first page and the system behind it. Rush timelines, unlimited revision clauses, and multi-language versions all move the number more than page count does.

sections.h2: How to tell if the quote you received is reasonable
paragraphs: Read it for these eight things, in this order. First: does it say who writes the copy? If it does not, you write it. Second: does it name a page count and a revision limit? Unlimited revisions are never free, they are priced in, and open-ended revision rounds are how projects die. Third: what happens after launch? Who hosts it, who updates it, what does a change cost, and how fast do they respond?

Fourth: do you own everything? The domain, the hosting account, the analytics property, and the content should be in your name, in your accounts. Fifth: can you leave? If the site cannot be exported or moved, the low monthly price is a lease, not a purchase, and you will find that out on the day you want to go somewhere else.

Sixth: is there a launch date, and does it mean anything? Seventh: does anything in the quote connect the site to how you actually get paid, or does the scope end at the words 'site is live'? A site that does not feed your follow-up is a business card that costs four figures. Eighth: ask for two sites they built more than a year ago, then check whether those sites are still live, still fast, and still turning up in search.

The red flags are just as useful. A five-figure quote with no copywriting line item. A $500 quote from someone who never asked what you sell or who buys it. A monthly plan with no exit and no export. 'SEO included' with no specifics attached to it. And any quote that arrives before anyone has looked at your current site or asked how you currently get customers.
If a quote clears those eight questions, the number is probably fair for what it is. If it fails four of them, the number is irrelevant because you are not buying what you think you are buying.

sections.h2: Squarespace, Wix, GoDaddy, Framer, Canva, and WordPress
paragraphs: Squarespace and Wix are the default DIY answer for good reason. Business plans generally sit in the $16 to $45 a month range on annual billing, hosting and certificates are included, and the templates are genuinely good now. The limits are structural: you are working inside their system, deep customization gets awkward, and moving off later means rebuilding.

GoDaddy's builder is cheap on the headline and the money is in the additions. Email, security, backups, privacy, and marketing tools are frequently sold separately, and a $10 a month plan can quietly become $40. Read the renewal terms specifically, because the first-term discount and the renewal rate are often very far apart.

Framer and Webflow are the designer-grade options, usually $15 to $40 a month per site, and they give you real control over how the thing looks and behaves. They also have a learning curve that most owners will not enjoy climbing on a Sunday. Canva's website feature is free with a subscription you may already have, and it is fine for a single landing page. It is weak on the structure search engines want, so treat it as a placeholder rather than a foundation.

WordPress is the most misunderstood number in this whole category. The software is free. The website is not. You pay for hosting, usually a premium theme at $50 to $100 once, plugins that are often billed annually, and either your time or someone else's on maintenance. It is enormously capable and it is not the free option people think it is.

And on Google specifically: Google Sites is free and is a reasonable internal tool, not a storefront. Google retired the free websites it used to generate from Business Profiles, and those addresses now point back at the profile itself. So if that was your plan, it is not on the table anymore. What is still on the table, and still free, is the Business Profile, which I covered in [do I need a website for my business](/blog/do-i-need-a-website-for-my-business/).

sections.h2: Ecommerce is a different question
paragraphs: An online store is a different animal from a brochure site, and the price reflects it. Shopify's standard plans run roughly $29 to $79 a month depending on tier, and WooCommerce on WordPress is free as software but carries the hosting and extension costs described above. A serious custom store build usually lands in the $3,000 to $15,000 range, and complex catalogs go well past that.

The cost driver in ecommerce is almost never the design. It is the products. Photography, descriptions, variants, sizing, shipping rules, and tax setup are per-product work, and a store with 400 SKUs is a data project with a website attached to it. Budget for that work or you will launch a beautiful store with twelve products in it.

Then there is the cut on every sale. Card processing across the major providers sits right around 2.9 percent plus 30 cents per transaction, and marketplace or platform fees stack on top of that depending on where you sell. That is not a build cost, it is a permanent margin cost, and it belongs in your math from day one.

If you are selling a service rather than products, you almost certainly do not need a store. You need a booking flow and an invoice, which is a much smaller build and a much smaller bill. I went through the sane version of that in [how to automate your invoicing](/blog/automate-invoicing/).

sections.h2: The costs that never appear on the invoice
paragraphs: Your time is the big one. A first-time DIY build realistically takes 40 to 80 hours once you count the writing, the photos, the fiddling, and the second attempt after you decide you hate the first one. Put your own hourly value on that. If an hour of your time in the field is worth $75, a 60 hour DIY build cost you $4,500 of billable capacity to avoid a $3,000 invoice. That math flips for a lot of owners once they actually run it.

The second hidden cost is the site that exists but does not convert. It is not a one-time loss, it is a small leak every single week, and it compounds quietly for years. Nobody sends you an invoice for the enquiries you did not get.

The third is delay. Every month without a working presence is a month of people checking you out, finding nothing or finding something stale, and calling someone else. That cost is invisible because the person who did not call you never told you they existed.

The fourth is the money that goes out the back once traffic starts arriving. Leads with no follow-up, quotes that never get chased, invoices that go out late. I put the full list in [where small businesses actually leak money](/blog/business-money-leaks/), and it is worth reading before you spend anything on a website, because a site that doubles your leads also doubles whatever you were already dropping.

sections.h2: A website is not the purchase. The pipeline is.
paragraphs: Here is the reframe that saves people the most money. A website is one component in a chain: someone finds you, decides you are credible, reaches out, gets a fast answer, gets a quote, pays, and gets updated. A beautiful site attached to a broken chain produces nothing. A plain site attached to a working chain produces work.

So the right question is not how much a website costs. It is which link in your chain is weakest right now. If nobody can find you, the money goes to search presence first. If people find you and do not reach out, the money goes to the site and the proof on it. If people reach out and you answer three days later, the money goes to follow-up before either.

The only numbers I have any right to show you come from a real California field-services company where I built and ran all of this before offering it to anyone: 705 jobs coordinated through the system, and organic traffic up 60 percent in 28 days with no ad spend. Those are that company's numbers, not this site's, and I say that plainly because most people quoting results are not that specific about whose results they are.

The point of that example is not the percentage. It is that the site, the search presence, and the follow-up were built as one thing. Bought separately, in the wrong order, from three different vendors, they cost more and do less.

sections.h2: What I charge, and why there is no price list on this page
paragraphs: I quote per project after looking at the business, and I am not going to put a fake number here to win a search result. The same five-page site is a $2,000 job for one business and an $8,000 job for another, and the difference is real: whether the copy exists, whether there are usable photos, whether anything has to connect to a calendar or an invoicing system, and whether the current site can be improved instead of replaced.

What I can tell you is what I refuse to do. I do not quote before I have looked at what you already have. I do not sell a site that ends at 'it is live'. And I do not build a site that you cannot take with you, because the domain and the accounts are yours from the first day.

What the build includes is on [the websites page](/services/websites/): a conversion-first site, wired into your follow-up, set up to be found, hosted and maintained so you never open a code editor. One person builds it, and that person answers the email.

If you want to know what your specific site should cost, send me the URL or tell me what you do, and I will tell you straight whether you need a rebuild, a tune-up, or nothing at all. That is free, and sometimes the honest answer is that you should spend the money somewhere else. [Start here](/get-started/), or email jesse@jessemoraga.com.

faq.q: How much does a website cost per month?
faq.a: On a DIY builder, roughly $16 to $45 a month on an annual plan, with hosting and certificates included. On WordPress, $5 to $50 a month for hosting plus whatever maintenance costs you. On a done-for-you arrangement, a monthly usually covers hosting, updates, and changes, and typically sits somewhere between $50 and $300 depending on how much changes and how fast you need it changed. Ask exactly what a change request costs before you sign anything monthly.

faq.q: How much does a website cost per year to run?
faq.a: For most small businesses, $200 to $1,500 a year once it is built. The floor is a domain at $10 to $20 plus a builder subscription. The ceiling includes managed hosting, business email for a few users, a maintenance plan, and a few paid plugins or apps. If someone quotes you an annual running cost above that for a standard service business site, ask them to itemize it.

faq.q: How much does a .com domain cost?
faq.a: Usually $10 to $20 a year at a mainstream registrar. Watch the renewal rate rather than the promotional first year, since the two are often very different. Premium or already-owned domains are a separate market and can run from hundreds to five figures. Whatever you pay, make sure it is registered in your name and in an account you control, because a domain sitting in a developer's account is a problem you only discover at the worst possible moment.

faq.q: How much does a website designer or developer charge?
faq.a: Experienced freelancers in the United States commonly bill $75 to $150 an hour, and a small business site is usually 20 to 60 hours of work, which is where the $1,000 to $5,000 project range comes from. Agencies bill higher, often through a project fee rather than an hourly rate. Below about $50 an hour you are generally paying for template assembly rather than design or strategy, which is sometimes exactly what you need and should be priced accordingly.

faq.q: How much does a website cost on Squarespace, Wix, or GoDaddy?
faq.a: The subscription itself is roughly $16 to $45 a month on annual billing for a business tier, with hosting and certificates included. GoDaddy in particular sells email, backups, security, and privacy as separate additions, so the real total is often well above the advertised plan price. Add $10 to $20 a year for the domain. If you hire someone to build on one of these platforms for you, that design work is a separate one-time cost, commonly $800 to $3,500.

faq.q: How much should a website audit or redesign cost?
faq.a: A genuine audit, meaning someone reviews your speed, structure, content, search presence, and conversion path and hands you a prioritized list, typically runs $300 to $1,500. A full redesign is priced like a new build because it usually is one. Be careful with free audits that are really sales documents: a real one tells you which things not to fix. I will look at a site and tell you what is costing you bookings without charging for it, and if the answer is a tune-up rather than a rebuild, that is what I will say.

blog.title: Do I Need a Website for My Business? An Honest Answer
blog.title_tag: Do I Need a Website for My Business? | ART3RY
blog.meta_description: Not always. You do not need one to be on Google, and a claimed profile plus referrals beats a bad site. Here is when the answer is yes, and when it is not yet.
blog.dek: A claimed Google profile and a strong referral flow will carry some businesses a long way. Here is exactly where that runs out, and what the smallest useful website really looks like.

sections.h2: The short answer, including when it is no
paragraphs: You do not need a website to exist on Google, to take payments, or to run a profitable business. Plenty of trades run for years on a claimed Google Business Profile, good reviews, and referrals. If that is you and you are booked, I will tell you to keep your money rather than sell you a site.

You need a website at the moment strangers have to decide about you without talking to you first. That is the whole test. Referrals arrive pre-trusted, so they need very little from you. A stranger who found you in a search has three or four competitors open in other tabs and is deciding in about fifteen seconds which of you looks like a real operating business.
So the honest version is: a Google Business Profile plus a strong referral flow beats a bad website, every time. A good website beats both, because it is the only asset in that list you actually own.

The rest of this page is where the line sits. What a profile does and where it stops, when the answer is genuinely 'not yet', when it is an obvious yes, and what the smallest website that actually works looks like.

sections.h2: No, you do not need a website to be on Google
paragraphs: This is the most common misunderstanding I run into, so let me be blunt about it. A Google Business Profile is free, it does not require a website, and it is what puts you in the map results. You claim it, you verify it, and you are on Google. The website field on the profile is optional and you can leave it empty.

Verification is the part that trips people up, not the website. Depending on your category and history, Google verifies by postcard, phone, email, or video, and video verification is increasingly common for service businesses. Until verification completes, you will not appear, and that has nothing to do with whether you have a site.

You can also point that website field at something other than a website: a booking page, a Facebook page, a scheduling link. It works. What you lose is a real destination where you control what a stranger reads about you, and one of the clearer relevance signals you can send about what you actually do and where.

One thing that is no longer an option: Google used to generate a free single-page website from your Business Profile, and it retired that. Those addresses now point back at the profile itself. If the plan was to lean on the free Google-built site, that plan is gone. The mechanics of getting found locally are in [SEO for local business](/blog/seo-for-local-business/).

sections.h2: What a Google Business Profile does, and where it runs out
paragraphs: A profile is genuinely powerful. It wins the map pack, it holds your reviews, it shows hours and photos, it takes calls and direction requests and messages, and it costs nothing. For a lot of local service businesses it is the single highest-return thing you own, and if yours is not claimed and filled out, do that before you read another word about websites.

Where it runs out is specificity. A profile cannot make your case at length. It cannot explain a process that justifies charging more than the cheapest option. It cannot host the answer to the awkward question that loses you jobs. It cannot show a stranger the six photos of similar work that would have closed them.

It also cannot rank for questions. Somebody typing 'plumber near me' will find your profile. Somebody typing what a specific job usually costs, or whether a permit is needed, or how long a thing takes, will find whoever wrote the answer. Those searches are earlier in the decision and they are where you become the obvious choice before anyone compares prices.

And you do not own it. A suspension, a category change, a competitor filing edits, and your presence changes without your consent. If the profile is your only address, a bad week at Google is a bad quarter in your business. Keeping it current is worth automating, which I covered in [local SEO automation](/blog/local-seo-automation/).

sections.h2: When the honest answer is 'not yet'
paragraphs: You are brand new and have no completed work. A website made entirely of adjectives converts worse than no website at all, because a visitor can feel the absence of proof. Do five jobs, take real photos, ask all five for a review, and then build. You will build a better site in a month than you would today, and it will cost you the same.

You are booked to capacity. A website's job is to create demand. If you are turning work away, more demand is not your constraint and a site will not help. Raise your prices, tighten your scheduling, or fix the part of the job that eats your evenings. Come back to the website when you have room.

You cannot finish this sentence: 'I do X for Y, and it usually takes Z.' If the offer is not clear in your own head, a website just publishes the confusion at scale. Every unclear site I have ever been asked to fix was an unclear offer first, and no amount of design fixed it.

Cash is genuinely tight. In that case, the order is: claim and complete the Google profile, get email on your own domain, put ten real photos of your work somewhere public, and build a habit of asking every finished customer for a review. That stack costs almost nothing and outperforms a $4,000 site for a business at that stage. It also builds the raw material the site will need later.

sections.h2: When it is a yes, and it is not close
paragraphs: You are paying for traffic. If you spend on ads, or buy leads from a platform, every dollar sends someone to a page. If that page is a profile you do not control or a competitor's marketplace listing, you are renting an audience and handing back the relationship. Paid traffic without a destination you own is the most expensive mistake in this category.

Your work needs explaining. Higher-ticket, technical, or unfamiliar services get researched before anybody calls. If your customer has to understand something before they are comfortable buying, that understanding has to live somewhere, and a profile has nowhere to put it.

Your competitors show up and you do not. Search a few of the things your customers actually type. If three competitors have pages answering those questions and you appear only when someone types your business name, you are invisible for every search that is not already about you.

You want inbound to enter a system instead of a voicemail. A website form that lands in a follow-up sequence beats a missed call every time, especially outside business hours. Pair it with something that answers when you cannot, and the after-hours enquiry stops evaporating. That is the argument in [what an AI receptionist actually is](/blog/what-is-an-ai-receptionist/).

And you want to stop being a tenant. Profiles, marketplaces, and social pages are all ground you rent. A domain you own with your content on it is the only piece of this that cannot be taken away by someone else's policy change.

sections.h2: Trust is the conversion mechanism, not design
paragraphs: A stranger landing on your site is running four checks in a few seconds, in this order. Is this a real operating business? Do they do exactly my thing? Have they done it for somebody like me? What happens if I reach out? Everything that answers one of those questions earns its place, and everything else is decoration.

The things that answer them are unglamorous. Real photos of your actual work, not stock. A full name and a face. License, registration, or certification numbers if your trade has them. The service area stated plainly. Reviews quoted with names attached. A straight answer about price, even if that answer is a range or a reason you quote after seeing the job. A described process, step by step, so the reader knows what the first week looks like.

The things that do not answer them are the things most sites are made of. Stock photography of a smiling team that is not yours. Phrases like 'passionate about excellence'. A hero carousel. An awards badge nobody recognizes. A mission statement. None of this moves anyone, because none of it is checkable.

The single highest-converting element on most small business sites is a clear answer to 'what happens next'. Tell them you reply within a few hours, tell them what you will ask, tell them what it costs to find out. Uncertainty is what stops people, and specificity is what removes it.

sections.h2: Your site versus Facebook, Instagram, and the lead marketplaces
paragraphs: A Facebook page can rank, can hold reviews, and can convert. It also puts your storefront behind someone else's login prompt, buries your contact details in a layout you do not control, changes that layout without asking, and can be disabled with no appeal and no warning. If your entire business address is a Facebook page, you have a single point of failure that you cannot inspect.

The lead marketplaces are worse in a specific way. You pay for the lead, they sell the same lead to three of your competitors, and the customer's relationship stays with the platform. You are buying a race, not a customer. That model works for filling gaps in a schedule and does not work as a foundation.

The practical rule is simple: use platforms for reach, own the address people land on. Post on social, be in the map results, appear in the marketplaces if the math works. Send all of it to one place that belongs to you.

The cheapest ownership move has nothing to do with a website. Get email on your own domain. A quote arriving from a free webmail address and the same quote arriving from your business domain get read very differently, and the second one costs a few dollars a month.

sections.h2: A bad website is worse than no website
paragraphs: A visitor who finds nothing forms no opinion of you. A visitor who finds a neglected site concludes you are barely operating, and that conclusion is much harder to reverse. This is the one case where doing nothing genuinely beats doing something badly.

The failure list is consistent. A layout that breaks on a phone. A page that takes six seconds to load on cellular data. A copyright year three years old in the footer. A contact form that has never been tested and quietly goes nowhere. A phone number you changed. Pages that still say 'coming soon'. A template with another city's name still in the text. A chat widget nobody answers.

Run the test yourself, right now, honestly. Open your own site on your phone, off wifi, the way a customer standing in a parking lot would. Time how long it takes to load. Find your own contact details. Send yourself an enquiry and see whether it arrives and how long you take to answer it.

Most owners discover something broken in that five-minute test. Fixing what you find is cheaper than a rebuild and usually recovers more work than a redesign would, which is a large part of why I look at the existing site before quoting anything.

sections.h2: Cleaning, coaching, and bookkeeping specifically
paragraphs: Cleaning. Mostly local and map-driven, so a claimed profile with steady reviews carries you a long way with residential customers. The site earns its keep the moment you want commercial contracts, because a property manager or a facilities coordinator will not award a recurring contract off a Facebook page. They want to see insurance, a service checklist, and evidence you handle buildings. A simple quote form also ends the phone tag that kills residential bookings.

Coaching. Here the website is close to the whole business. There is no map pack to win and often no local intent at all, so nothing is putting you in front of anyone by geography. The entire sale is trust in a specific person, and that requires long-form: who you help, what changes for them, what it costs, what the first session looks like, and real testimonials from named people. One strong page with genuine proof beats a ten-page site with none.

Bookkeeping. Buyers are checking credibility and safety before anything else, because they are about to hand you access to their money. Credentials, the software you work in, a clearly scoped engagement, a real business email, and a plain statement of how you handle their data. This trade is heavily referral-driven, so the site's job is often to confirm a referral rather than generate one, and confirming a referral is worth a great deal since that is the visitor most likely to buy.

The pattern across all three: the more your customer has to trust you before they pay, the more the website matters. The more your customer decides by proximity and price, the more the profile matters.

sections.h2: The smallest website that actually works
paragraphs: One page is enough to start. At the top: what you do, who you do it for, where you do it, and one obvious action. Not a slogan. A sentence a stranger could repeat to somebody else correctly.

Then proof. Three to five photos of your real work, three reviews with names, and any license or certification number your trade uses. Then the services, written in the words customers use rather than the words your industry uses. Then price, handled honestly: a range, a starting-from, or a plain explanation of why you quote after seeing the job. Silence on price reads as expensive.

Then contact. One method that reaches you fast and one that captures after hours into something that follows up, so the eleven at night enquiry is still there in the morning. Then a footer with your legal business name, service area, and an email address on your own domain.

That is a weekend on a builder or a small paid build, and it will out-convert most of the expensive sites it sits next to. If you want the real numbers for each route, they are in [what a small business website actually costs](/blog/how-much-does-a-small-business-website-cost/). If you want it built and wired into your follow-up rather than left sitting there, that is [what I build](/services/websites/).

And if you are still not sure whether you need one, send me the name of your business and what you do. I will look at what you already have and tell you straight whether a site would earn its money or whether your money belongs somewhere else this quarter. [Start here](/get-started/), or email jesse@jessemoraga.com.

faq.q: Do I have to have a website for my business?
faq.a: No. There is no legal or platform requirement to have one, and businesses run profitably without one every day on referrals and a claimed Google profile. It becomes necessary at the point where people who have never met you are deciding whether to contact you, because that decision needs proof and a profile can only hold so much of it.

faq.q: Do I need a website for Google My Business?
faq.a: No. A Google Business Profile is free, does not require a website, and the website field on it is optional. You can leave it blank or point it at a booking link or a social page. Leaving it blank costs you clicks and a useful relevance signal, so it is not free of consequence, but it is not a blocker to being listed or verified.

faq.q: Do I need a website to put my business on Google?
faq.a: No. You claim and verify a Business Profile and you are on Google, usually within days once verification completes. If you are not showing up, the cause is almost always verification, category, or address settings rather than the absence of a site. Google also retired the free websites it used to build from profiles, so that shortcut no longer exists.

faq.q: Do I need a website for my cleaning business?
faq.a: For residential work, a claimed profile with consistent reviews will carry you a long way and should come first. For commercial contracts, yes, effectively. Property and facilities managers want to see insurance, a service checklist, and evidence you handle buildings before they will award recurring work, and none of that fits on a profile. A quote form also removes the phone tag that loses residential bookings.

faq.q: Do I need a website for my coaching or bookkeeping business?
faq.a: For coaching, yes, and it is close to the whole business, because there is no local map result to win and the sale is trust in a person that has to be built in long form. For bookkeeping, yes for a different reason: clients are about to give you access to their money and they will check credentials, scope, and how you handle data before they call. In both cases one strong page with real proof beats a large site with none.

faq.q: Is a Facebook page enough instead of a website?
faq.a: It can be, early on, and plenty of businesses start there. The risks are that it sits behind a login prompt, the layout and reach change without your say, and the page can be disabled with no appeal. Use it for reach and posting, and get an address you own as soon as the business can justify it, even if that address is a single well-built page.
